blocks.recap_md: Case analysis needs a new special form: `cond` tries clauses of the form `(⟨predicate⟩ ⟨expression⟩)` in order.
`cond` evaluates predicates left to right and returns the consequent of the first true one; `abs` uses the primitive predicates `>`, `<`, `=`.
`else` can replace the predicate in a `cond`'s final clause, matching whenever every earlier clause was bypassed.
`if` is a restricted two-case conditional: `(if ⟨predicate⟩ ⟨consequent⟩ ⟨alternative⟩)` evaluates exactly one of consequent/alternative based on the predicate.
`and`, `or`, and `not` let you build compound predicates; `and`/`or` are special forms (they short-circuit), while `not` is an ordinary procedure.
A range check uses `and`; `>=` can be defined either via `or` or via `not`, two equivalent formulations of the same predicate.
Exercises 1.1 and 1.2: evaluating a sequence of expressions by hand, and translating an arithmetic expression into prefix form.
Exercises 1.3-1.5: sum of squares of the two larger of three numbers, a procedure whose operator is itself a compound expression, and Ben Bitdiddle's applicative-order-vs-normal-order test.

knowledge_items.statement: `cond` evaluates its clauses' predicates in order and returns the value of the consequent expression for the first predicate that's true; a clause whose predicate is the special symbol `else` always matches when reached.
`if` is a restricted conditional for exactly two cases: it evaluates the predicate, then evaluates and returns either the consequent (if true) or the alternative (if false) - never both.

`and` and `or` are special forms, not ordinary procedures, because they don't necessarily evaluate all their subexpressions (`and` stops at the first false one, `or` stops at the first true one); `not` is an ordinary procedure.

questions.prompt: In `(cond ((> x 0) x) ((= x 0) 0) ((< x 0) (- x)))`, if x is 0, what value does the `cond` expression return?
options: 0, because the second clause's predicate `(= x 0)` is the first one that evaluates to true
x, because the first clause is always tried and its result is used regardless of the predicate
(- x), because the interpreter always evaluates the last clause first
The cond expression is undefined whenever more than one clause could conceivably be true
questions.explanation: cond tries each clause's predicate in order and returns the consequent of the first one that's true; here `(> x 0)` is false when x=0, but `(= x 0)` is true, so 0 is returned.

questions.prompt: For `(if (< x 0) (- x) x)`, if the predicate `(< x 0)` evaluates to false, what does the interpreter do?
options: It evaluates the alternative, `x`, and returns that value - it does not also evaluate the consequent `(- x)`
It evaluates both the consequent and the alternative and returns whichever is larger
It re-evaluates the predicate a second time to confirm before choosing a branch
It returns the predicate's own false value directly, without evaluating consequent or alternative
questions.explanation: if evaluates exactly one of consequent/alternative depending on the predicate's truth value - here, since the predicate is false, only the alternative `x` is evaluated and returned; `(- x)` is never touched.

questions.prompt: Why are `and` and `or` special forms rather than ordinary procedures?
options: Because they don't necessarily evaluate all of their subexpressions - `and` stops at the first false one, `or` stops at the first true one
Because they can only take exactly two arguments, unlike ordinary procedures
Because they must always be the outermost expression in a program
Because, unlike ordinary procedures, they aren't allowed to appear inside a `define`
questions.explanation: The text notes `and`/`or` are special forms precisely because their subexpressions aren't necessarily all evaluated (short-circuiting), unlike ordinary procedures (like `not`) which always evaluate all their arguments.
